vignette:
Javier holds his coffee mug with both hands, a practice he started a few months ago. He tells himself it’s because the ceramic is warm, a comfort on a cool morning. But he knows, and suspects his wife Elena knows, that it’s to conceal the fine tremor in his right hand. His right hand. The hand that has performed thousands of precise, life-saving maneuvers; the hand that once moved with the unthinking confidence of a master craftsman. Now, it feels like a stranger’s.

Before the earthquake, his life was one of order and control. The operating room was his sanctuary, a sterile, predictable world of beeps, hushed commands, and the elegant mechanics of the human body. He was Dr. Morales, a cardiothoracic surgeon whose reputation was built on steadiness and an almost intuitive grace with a scalpel. He loved the pressure, the feeling of holding a life in his hands and guiding it back from the brink. At home, he was the calm center of his family, the one who fixed things, the one who knew the answers.

He was in the middle of a complex bypass surgery when the world began to roar. It wasn't a shake, not at first. It was a deep, guttural sound that seemed to come from the center of the earth, followed by a violent lurch that threw his assisting nurse into a tray of instruments. The lights flickered, then died, plunging the OR into a terrifying darkness punctuated only by the failing battery backup of the monitors. The building groaned around them, a wounded beast. The controlled symphony of the OR devolved into chaos.

For the next 48 hours, Javier wasn't a surgeon; he was a battlefield medic in his own hospital. Working by flashlight and cell phone glow, he set bones, stitched gaping wounds, and performed amputations with equipment he would have deemed archaic just a day before. The sterile scent of his workplace was replaced by the thick, choking smell of concrete dust, blood, and fear. He had to make impossible triage decisions, placing a black tag on a colleague he’d had coffee with that morning, choosing to save a child over an adult whose injuries were too severe. He saw death on a scale he had never imagined, not as a singular, clinical event, but as a relentless, indiscriminate tide.

He and his family were lucky. Their home was damaged but standing. They were alive. Everyone told him he was a hero. But the man who returned to that house was not the one who had left it.

Sleep offers no refuge. He often jolts awake, heart pounding, the phantom sensation of the floor swaying beneath him. During the day, a passing truck can make his breath catch, his muscles tense for an impact that never comes. He finds himself scanning the ceilings of every room he enters, tracing the lines of support beams, mapping out escape routes.

The hospital, once his domain, now feels like a trap. The familiar beep of a heart monitor sounds less like a vital sign and more like a warning siren. He snaps at residents for minor mistakes and feels a growing, hollow distance from his patients. The intricate work he once loved now fills him with a quiet dread. What if his hand shakes? The thought is a constant, looping whisper. This fear has become a corrosive acid, eating away at the foundation of his identity.

He no longer tells Elena about his day. The chasm between his experience and the placid normalcy she tries to maintain feels too vast to bridge. He sees the worry in her eyes when he flinches at the sound of their children dropping a toy, or when he stares blankly at the television, the images of some distant disaster replaying the scenes from his own memory. He feels an irritable anger simmering just below the surface, an impatience with a world that has simply moved on. He is here, but he is also still there, in the dust and the dark, surrounded by the ghosts of the choices he had to make. The solid ground he had built his entire life upon was gone, and he was still in free fall.
